title: 26 % of the Netherlands lies below sea level
subtitle: A 50 × 60 cm print map in the manner of Nadieh Bremer's personal map of Norway: rivers and main canals as the featured layer, land below sea level hatched, height contours, a map-in-map of the Rhine and Maas basins
data: OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL), coastline, rivers, canals, water areas, borders and places, via the Overpass API, downloaded 2026-10-12; AHN4 DTM (Rijkswaterstaat and Het Waterschapshuis, via PDOK, CC0); AWS Terrain Tiles (Mapzen; SRTM, GMTED2010, ETOPO1); Natural Earth 10 m rivers, lakes and countries (public domain)
alt: A portrait print map of the Netherlands in Mercator projection. The country is white on a pale teal North Sea, its neighbours in cream. Land below sea level is hatched in teal: 26.4 % of the ground measured by AHN4, about 8 970 km², most of Holland, Flevoland, Friesland and Groningen. The Rhine enters from Germany and splits at the Pannerdensche Kop and the IJsselkop, marked in terracotta, into the Waal, Nederrijn–Lek and IJssel; with the Maas they are drawn in the deepest teal and thickest line, other rivers and canals thinner and lighter. Height contours rise to the Vaalserberg, 322 m; the lowest ground is −6.8 m in the Zuidplaspolder. A map-in-map shows the Rhine from the Alps and the Maas from France.
note: Every number is computed from data/maps/ (nl_stats.json, written by fetch_nl.py). Labels are set as glyph outlines, bent along rivers and water bodies where they follow a shape. Rasters (sea, land, hatching, shadows, lakes) are drawn at 200 dpi and embedded in the PDF; lines and type are vector.

title: The sea rose 39 m in 11,000 years, 31 m of it in the first 3,500, and turned the valleys of the Calanques into inlets
subtitle: Marseille to Cassis · relative sea level from 66 index points on the French Mediterranean coast (Vacchi et al. 2021) · ground from IGN RGE ALTI, sea floor from EMODnet
form: four-panel composite: relief map, index points with Gaussian-process fit, terrain section, three block diagrams
data: IGN RGE ALTI and EMODnet Bathymetry DTM for the Calanques coast; 66 sea-level index points from the Languedoc to Nice, Vacchi et al. (2021)
alt: Four panels on the Calanques coast near Marseille. a: a map from Marseille to Cassis with ground height and sea depth; the shore of 11,000 years ago follows the -39 m isobath a few hundred metres off today's cliffs. b: relative sea level from 66 index points on the French Mediterranean coast: -39 m 11,000 years ago, -8 m 7,500 years ago, then a slow rise to today; the sea reached the depth of the Cosquer cave entrance, 37 m, about 10,805 years ago. c: a section through Cap Morgiou: cliffs plunge from the slopes of Mont Puget to a sea floor 90 to 100 m down. d: three block diagrams of the same coast at sea levels of -39 m, -8 m and 0: a strip of land below the cliffs, then the sea against the cliffs, then the valleys flooded as inlets.
note: Index points of regions 9–14 of Vacchi et al. (2021): Languedoc, Rhône delta, Marseille, La Ciotat–Hyères, Fréjus and Cap Ferrat; the 7 older than 7,600 years are all from the Rhône delta, where compaction may lower them. Fit: a Gaussian process, squared-exponential kernel, amplitude 40 m and length scale 5 thousand years by maximum likelihood, age errors as extra height variance. The blocks keep today's ground: no sediment is removed or added, so they show where the sea stood, not the coast's full history. The Cosquer cave is placed on the −37 m contour nearest its published position; its entrance depth is from Clottes, Courtin and Vanrell (2005). Sea floor depths are referred to lowest astronomical tide, about 0.2 m below mean sea level at Marseille.
